rules.message: Async Express/router handler with no surrounding try/catch, `next(err)`, or `.catch()` — on Express 4, an unhandled rejection in an async handler crashes or hangs the process; Express 5 forwards async rejections to error-handling middleware automatically, so there it's a style/consistency concern rather than a crash bug. Wrap in try/catch and call `next(err)`, or attach `.catch(next)`. A route wrapped by error-handling middleware like `express-async-handler` or `express-async-errors` is also safe, but that wrapping isn't visible in the handler body this rule scans — the rule's biggest real-world false-positive source.

Synchronous fs/child_process call (`readFileSync`, `execSync`, etc.) alongside request-handler evidence (a `req.`/`request.` member access, or a response-API call like `res.status(...)`/`res.send(...)` — deliberately NOT `res.json(`/`res.text(`, which a fetch `Response` also has, so a handler whose only response evidence is a bare `res.json(x)` is accepted as a miss rather than risking fetch-response false positives) — a blocking call on the request path stalls Node's event loop for every concurrent request. Use the async `fs.promises`/`child_process` APIs, or move CPU-heavy work to a worker thread.

`.map(async ...)` used without wrapping the result in `Promise.all`/`Promise.allSettled` — `.map` returns pending Promises, so a rejection becomes unhandled and any ordering/completion guarantee is lost. Wrap the call in `Promise.all(...)` (or `Promise.allSettled(...)` for expected partial failures).

Debug flag or disabled TLS verification (`debug: true`, `NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0`, `rejectUnauthorized: false`) committed to source — ships a dev backdoor or TLS bypass to production if deployed unchanged. The two TLS shapes are Node-specific, but the `debug: true` shape is not, and this rule scans Rust as well: a struct literal (`Settings { debug: true }`) fires exactly as a JS object literal does. Remove the flag, or gate it behind an environment check in whichever language the line is written in — `process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production'` in Node, `std::env::var` in Rust. Suppress a vetted line with `// zzop-debug-true-committed-ok`.

`Promise.all(...)` used with DB write calls on a DB-client-shaped receiver (`prisma`/`db`/`tx`/`client`/`repo`) — non-atomic: some writes land and others don't when one rejects, with no rollback for what committed. Wrap the writes in a transaction, or use `Promise.allSettled(...)` with compensation logic. Co-occurrence heuristic, not proof — it flags a `Promise.all(...)` and a write call in the same function, not that the writes are actually inside the `Promise.all(...)` array; confirm before acting.

`JSON.parse(...)` called directly on apparent external input (`req`/`body`/`params`/`query`/`payload`/`event`) without a surrounding `try` — malformed input throws, turning a bad request into a 500 or a process crash. Wrap the parse in try/catch and return a proper 4xx on failure.

Outbound HTTP call (`fetch`/`axios`/`got`) in server/worker code with no timeout or `AbortController` visible in the same function — `fetch` has no default timeout, so a hung upstream hangs the request and can exhaust the connection pool. Pass an explicit timeout (e.g. `AbortSignal.timeout(...)`) or wire up an `AbortController`. A timeout set on a shared client instance in another file (e.g. `axios.create({ timeout })` in a helper module) isn't visible to this per-function check — this is the rule's biggest real-world false-positive vector.

A `reqwest` HTTP client is constructed inside this function (`Client::new()` / `Client::builder()` / `Client::default()` / `ClientBuilder::new()`, or the `reqwest::get(url)` convenience call — which builds a fresh, timeout-less default client on every invocation — in a file that names `reqwest` at all) and no `.timeout(` call appears in the same function body — reqwest's default client has no request timeout, so a peer that accepts the connection and then stalls holds this task, its connection and whatever it borrows for as long as the peer likes. Set one: `Client::builder().timeout(Duration::from_secs(5)).build()`, or `.timeout(..)` on the individual request builder; for `reqwest::get` there is no builder to put one on — construct a client instead. Scope, disclosed rather than assumed: the veto is FUNCTION-LOCAL, purely lexical, and matches the METHOD spellings `.timeout(` and `.read_timeout(` only — so a client built by a shared constructor elsewhere and merely used here is invisible to it, a timeout configured outside this function reads as absent, and a caller-side deadline such as `tokio::time::timeout(...)` does not clear it either (use the suppression marker for that case) — confirm before changing code. `read_timeout` DOES clear it: it bounds exactly the stalled-peer read this message describes. `connect_timeout` deliberately does NOT clear it: that caps the HANDSHAKE only, and the stalled-peer failure above begins after the handshake succeeds. The TypeScript sibling is `reliability/fetch-no-timeout`.

Body parser (`express.json`/`urlencoded`, `bodyParser.json`/`urlencoded`) configured without an explicit `limit` — the code relies on the implicit 100kb default, which is too small for some legitimate endpoints and simply unexamined for the rest. Set an explicit `limit` (e.g. `{ limit: '1mb' }`) sized to the endpoint's needs.

`setInterval(...)` with no matching `clearInterval(...)` anywhere in this file — a leaked timer keeps the process (or page) alive and re-fires forever, since nothing cancels it. Store the return value in a handle and call `clearInterval(handle)` during teardown/cleanup.

A file/stream handle (`fs.createReadStream(`/`fs.createWriteStream(`/`fs.open(`/`fs.openSync(`) is opened structurally inside a loop body — verified against the parser's projected loop spans (the open call's own line falls within a loop statement's or array-iteration callback's span), not merely co-occurring with loop syntax somewhere in the same function — and the enclosing function never closes it (`.close(`/`.destroy(`/`pipeline(`/`finished(` anywhere in the function). Under a fan-out, the file descriptors accumulate across iterations and the process eventually hits `EMFILE: too many open files`. Note honestly: the close-absence check is whole-function scoped and matches `.close(`/`.destroy(`/`pipeline(`/`finished(` on ANY object — so a close inside a sibling branch or a callee is invisible here and the finding still fires (false positive), while an unrelated `res.close()`/`conn.destroy()` elsewhere in the function vetoes a genuine stream leak (false negative); verify before refactoring. Close the handle in a `finally` block, or use `pipeline(...)`, which closes both ends automatically.

An EventEmitter listener (`.on('event',…)`/`.once(`/`.addListener(`/`.prependListener(`, anchored on a string event-name argument) is registered structurally inside a loop body — verified against the parser's projected loop spans (the subscribe call's own line falls within a loop statement's or array-iteration callback's span), not merely co-occurring with loop syntax somewhere in the same function — with no matching removal (`.off(`/`.removeListener(`/`.removeAllListeners(`) anywhere in the enclosing function. To avoid firing on same-shaped non-EventEmitter `.on('...')` calls (a frontend DOM/jQuery `$(el).on('click', …)`, a knex join builder, a D3 selection), the rule only scans files that use a Node event-emitter/server library (an `events`/`net`/`http`/`ws`/`socket.io`/... import, or a `.setMaxListeners(` call). This is the event-listener sibling of `interval-no-clear` (which covers `setInterval`): listeners pile up on every iteration, Node warns `MaxListenersExceeded`, and each event then fires the handler N times (duplicate side effects, unbounded memory growth). Note honestly: the removal-absence check is whole-function scoped — a teardown living in a different function (or an unrelated `.off(` on another object) either misses a real fix or vetoes a real leak; verify before refactoring. Register the listener once outside the loop, or collect the listeners and remove them during teardown.

`await` used directly inside a `Promise.all(...)`/`Promise.allSettled(...)`/`Promise.race(...)` array literal — each awaited element resolves before the next element of the array is even evaluated, so the calls run one after another instead of concurrently, silently defeating the whole point of `Promise.all`. This is syntax-proven where it fires: an `await` textually between the array's `[` and `]` on the SAME line always serializes that element against the next (the line-scan only sees the single-line form — a multi-line array with each `await` on its own line is not flagged). Move the `await` out — build the array of un-awaited promises first, then await the combinator once (e.g. `Promise.all([getA(), getB()])`, or `await Promise.all(items.map((i) => getA(i)))`).

An `async` callback registered as an EventEmitter listener (`.on`/`.once`/`.addListener`/`.prependListener`) — the emitter fires it and discards the returned promise, so a rejection inside the handler becomes an unhandled promise rejection, which crashes the process on Node 15+ (and is a silent swallow on older Node). The rule only scans files that use a Node event-emitter/server library (an `events`/`net`/`http`/`ws`/... import, or a `.setMaxListeners(` call), so a frontend DOM `el.on('click', async …)` is not flagged. Wrap the handler body in try/catch and log/handle the error there, or wrap the callback so its promise is observed (e.g. a small `catchAsync(fn)` helper).

A create/write call (`fs.writeFile`/`fs.open`/`fs.rename`/...) appears LEXICALLY AFTER a filesystem existence/permission check (`fs.existsSync`/`fs.access`/`fs.stat`/...) in the NEAREST enclosing function, with no exclusive-create flag (`wx`/`O_EXCL`) visible anywhere in it — CWE-367 TOCTOU: between the check and the use, the path can be swapped out from under it (e.g. via a symlink) or another writer can win the race, so the check is stale by the time the write happens. A trigger line that sits inside NO parser-projected function span (a class-property initializer, a top-level statement) is read as ungated, and the pairing there widens back to the whole scanned symbol span. The order is TEXTUAL, and path identity is not checked at all: it does not confirm the check and the write target the same path, nor that both run on the same control-flow path (`fs.existsSync(a)` followed by `fs.writeFile(b)` still fires). SAME-LINE NESTING RESIDUAL (a disclosed false negative shared by every rule that uses this order gate): on a single line "after" is decided by MATCH START OFFSET, so a check nested INSIDE the write call's own argument list reads as coming AFTER it and does not pair — `fs.writeFileSync(p, data, { flag: fs.existsSync(p) ? 'a' : 'w' });` is silently NOT reported, while the ordinary one-liner `if (!fs.existsSync(p)) fs.writeFileSync(p, data);` (check first) fires. Prefer opening with an exclusive-create flag (`{ flag: 'wx' }` in Node, `O_EXCL` at the syscall level), which fails atomically if the path already exists instead of trusting a separate check.

An `await`ed Node `fs`/`fs.promises` call (`readFile`/`writeFile`/`appendFile`/`unlink`/`rename`/`copyFile`/`mkdir`/`rm`/`readdir`/`stat`/`access`/... — deliberately excluding `open`/`createReadStream`/`createWriteStream`, which `stream-open-no-close-in-loop` already covers for the handle-leak angle) executes structurally inside a loop body — verified against the parser's projected loop spans (the call's own line falls within a loop statement's or array-iteration callback's span), not merely co-occurring with loop syntax somewhere in the same function — with no `Promise.all`/`Promise.allSettled` anywhere in the enclosing function. Each iteration's disk I/O waits for the previous one to finish before starting, serializing work the filesystem would otherwise run concurrently; over many files this adds up to iteration-count times the single-call latency. This generalizes `map-async-no-promise-all` (which only catches the `.map(async ...)` callback shape) to the ordinary `for`/`for-of`/`for-in`/`while` loop forms, scoped to `fs` I/O specifically — database calls in a loop are `sql/nplus1`'s territory and outbound network calls are `perf/api-in-loop`'s, both already covering their own receivers, so this rule only anchors on an `fs`/`fsPromises`/`fsp`/`fs.promises`-shaped receiver to stay out of their way. Gather the paths up front and run the calls concurrently with `Promise.all(...)` (bounded by a concurrency limiter if the fan-out is large), or use a single directory-level/batch operation where the API allows it. Suppress a vetted case (e.g. deliberately sequential writes to preserve on-disk ordering) with `// zzop-fs-in-loop-serial-ok`.
